title: groupby: summarising each group

cells.text: Last lesson you found the average price of **all** games. But what about the average price **per genre**? That's what `groupby()` does. It's the same idea as GROUP BY in SQL.

cells.prompt: Press Run to load the games table.
cells.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("games.csv")
df.head()

cells.text: `df.groupby("genre")["price"].mean()` reads in 3 parts: **groupby("genre")** makes one group per genre, **["price"]** picks the column to summarise, and **.mean()** works out the average in each group. You get one row per genre.

cells.prompt: There are 11 different genres. How many rows will the result have? Pick one, then press Run.

cells.text: You can group by any column and use any summary: `sum()`, `min()`, `max()`, `count()` and so on.

cells.prompt: Replace ___ with "release_year" (in quotes) to find the best rating in each release year, then press Run.
hints: The column to group by goes in quotes.

cells.prompt: Your turn: count how many games each genre has, using groupby. Group by genre, pick the title column, then count().

cells.text: To get several summaries at once, use `agg()` with a list of their names in quotes: `.agg(["min", "max", "mean"])`. You get one column per summary.

cells.prompt: Press Run to see the lowest, highest and average rating per genre, rounded to 2 decimals.
For each genre, show the cheapest and the most expensive price.
hints: Group by genre, pick price, then .agg() with a list of 2 names.

cells.text: You can keep adding steps at the end: `.round(2)` to tidy decimals, then `.sort_values(ascending=False)` to put the biggest first.

cells.prompt: Last one: show the average price per studio_id, rounded to 2 decimals, highest first.
hints: Group, pick, mean, then add .round(2) and .sort_values(ascending=False) on the end.

recap: groupby("col")["other"].mean() summarises each group. agg([...]) gives several summaries at once. Add .round() and .sort_values() to tidy the result.
